newsitem.title: USA: U.S. will not pressure Japan on N.Korea aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will not pressure Japan on N.Korea aid.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it will not pressure Japan to donate more food aid to North Korea at a meeting next week in Tokyo despite a worsening food crisis that could produce starvation in 11 weeks.
John Dinger, a State Department spokesman, confirmed the food situation in North Korea would be on the agenda when senior U.S., South Korean and Japanese officials meet on Wednesday in Tokyo.

Many have criticised Japan for holding back on additional food aid contributions at a time when humanitarian groups say North Korea is facing famine. Japan has held back partly due to anger over charges that North Korea kidnapped a Japanese school girl in 1977 and spirited her to Pyongyang.

Representative Tony Hall, who just visited North Korea, told a State Department audience that a doctor in his delegation estimated "on the current ration of 500 calories a day, the average woman in North Korea will become severely wasted in 11 to 12 weeks ... the average North Korean man has 14 to 16 weeks."

Hall, an Ohio Democrat, added: "Of course, conditions have worsened steadily since 1992 and the International Red Cross says people are no longer getting even that minimum ration. So his (the doctor's) estimate is probably conservative."

He called for larger donations. "Waiting makes solutions more complicated and less effective and far more expensive ... Waiting almost certainly will not improve the behaviour of North Korea's (Stalinist) government," he said.

Hall said Japan has not contributed any food aid this year and while acknowledging that Pyongyang "has a lot to answer for" argued that its people should not be "damn(ed) ... to the hell of a severe famine" because of events 20 years ago.

"Japan's delay in answering the U.N. appeal is made more puzzling by the fact that they have three or four million tons of food on reserve. But they also have about ... 350,000 tons of surplus rice that at this time is just going to waste," Hall said.
The United States, the largest food aid donor to North Korea, has said it would consider additional appeals from the U.N. World Food Programme if they are made, a point Dinger reiterated on Friday.
But as for trying to influence Tokyo, Dinger told a news briefing, "we have made very clear that this (food aid) is a decision for the Japanese government to make."
The chief U.S. official at next week's Tokyo meeting, Acting Assistant Secretary of State Charles Kartman, "is not going to pressure Japan into providing food aid," Dinger said.

Talks between the United States, South Korea and its arch-rival North Korea stalled in New York last month over the issue of food aid. Pyongyang said it was willing to accept a U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks but only if certain conditions -- increased food aid, lifting U.S. economic sanctions and diplomatic recognition -- were met.
The aim of the four-party talks, which would also include China, is to close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing a frayed armistice with a permanent peace treaty.
The U.S., South Korea, Japan meeting will focus on how to make progress on the peace talks proposal.

The three countries have been closely cooperating on North Korea, and holding regular trilateral meetings, since Pyongyang and Washington in 1994 signed a landmark agreement under which the North agreed to freeze its nuclear programme in return for $4.5 billion in nuclear technology and alternative energy supplies. Seoul and Tokyo are paying most of that cost.

Despite Dinger's comments, the chief State Department spokesman, Nicholas Burns, when asked about Japan, said several times recently that Washington believes North Korea's food crisis is urgent and all countries should contribute.
The crisis has been caused by systemic problems associated with Pyongyang's Stalinist regime compounded by several years of flooding, experts say.
